title: Cicero on duties
hookLine: Cicero, not a Stoic himself, wrote On Duties drawing on Panaetius (On Duties 1)

lines: A FATHER WRITES TO HIS SON.
A BOOK ON HOW TO LIVE.
cards: A father writes to his son, who's away at university in another country. The son, the letters hint, has been spending more time at parties than in lectures.

The father's city has just been through an assassination, and danger is closing in around him. He doesn't write a scolding letter. He writes a book, in three parts, on how to live as a decent person in public life.
It will outlast him by a long way.

teach.h: CICERO: NOT A STOIC, A BORROWER.
teach.b: First, the writer. Marcus Tullius Cicero was a Roman orator and statesman, and not a Stoic.

In philosophy he belonged to the Academy, the school descended from Plato, which taught that we should hold our views with caution. But he admired the Stoics' ethics, and he borrowed freely. Second, the moment.

In 44 BC, after Julius Caesar was assassinated, Cicero wrote On Duties for his son, also named Marcus, who was studying in Athens. Three parts: what is honorable; what is useful; what to do when the two seem to clash.
Third, the borrowing. For the first two parts, Cicero says plainly that he's following Panaetius, but as his own judge, not just as a translator.
Panaetius had promised a third part on the clash between honor and usefulness, and never wrote it. Cicero did. His answer is firm: a thing that's truly dishonorable can never really be useful.
If it looks useful, you're looking wrong. Fourth, the cost. A year later, Cicero was killed on the orders of Mark Antony, whom he had attacked in speeches.
He didn't get to see what his son became.

teach.h: 44 BC: A BOOK FOR HIS SON.
teach.b: But the book lasted; readers kept copying and studying it long after Rome fell.
The Latin word in the title, officium, means duty, but also service, a job done for others.
A duty, to Cicero, wasn't a weight.
It was what a person owes as a citizen, a friend, a parent.

how: Students of ethics and political thought read Cicero's On Duties as a guide to public and private obligation, and as a main window onto the Stoic idea of fitting action.

o: duty as a service owed to others
a rule enforced by Roman law courts
a public office held by a Roman senator

games.q: Cicero on duties. tap the pairs.
p: his main source for parts one and two

s: he belonged to the Academy, though he admired and borrowed Stoic ethics.
Panaetius promised a part on honor versus usefulness and never wrote it
Cicero wrote that third part himself.
Cicero says something dishonorable can sometimes be truly useful
his answer is that the truly dishonorable is never truly useful.

games.q: you're Cicero, and Panaetius never wrote the part on honor versus usefulness. what do you do?
games.why: Cicero wrote book three himself, arguing that what is truly dishonorable is never truly useful.

practice: Run through the roles you hold right now: child, parent, partner, coworker, neighbor, friend. Pick one and ask Cicero's question: what does this role ask of me today?
Let the answer be one specific duty, like picking up the phone or listening without the screen, and picture yourself doing it well, the way you'd want it done for you.

wordCard.voice: Officium. Cicero's Latin word for duty: a service owed to others, as a citizen, a friend, a parent. Today's word.

orig.note: Latin: duty, service, a job owed to others. Cicero's word for the Greek kathēkon.
